slides.name: The air our children breathe

layers.name: Toxic air is a school-gate p

params.text: Toxic air is a school-gate problem.

layers.name: children in England go to sc

params.text: children in England go to school where the air is toxic
more likely: a London child’s school is above WHO pollution limits
lower lung function among children in Tower Hamlets
THE AIR POLLUTION PROJECT  ·  MARK MARTIN MBE

slides.notes:
Three clicks, three numbers. Let each one land before the next.

3.1 million children in England go to schools in areas with toxic air. Children in London are almost four times more likely to attend a school where pollution exceeds the World Health Organization limit. In Tower Hamlets, children's lung function is around 5% below the national average (Tower Hamlets "Breathe Clean").

Check the sources are still current before presenting.

slides.name: When the air reaches the hospital

layers.name: When the air reaches the hos

params.text: When the air reaches the hospital
children in London taken to A&E or admitted to hospital with serious breathing problems in a single year

layers.name: of them admitted to a hospit

params.text: of them admitted to a hospital ward
A little inflammation can close down a child’s breathing.
Bronchiolitis, severe asthma attacks and pneumonia.
41% higher admission rates for respiratory infections in England’s most deprived areas.
Sources: Mums for Lungs FOI research with London NHS trusts (Aug 2025); Impact on Urban Health, NHS Hospital Episode Statistics 2024/25, under-18s in England
THE AIR POLLUTION PROJECT  ·  MARK MARTIN MBE

slides.notes:
Bring it into the hospital. Mums for Lungs' Freedom of Information research with London NHS trusts (published August 2025): around 120,000 children were taken to A&E or admitted to hospital in London in a year with serious breathing problems — about 85,000 A&E attendances and 35,000 admissions. Some trusts didn't respond, so it's likely an undercount. (Click for the 35,000.)

Why children: their airways are smaller, so a little inflammation from a cold or virus can restrict breathing. The main drivers are bronchiolitis (under-2s), severe asthma attacks and pneumonia.

Where they live matters: Impact on Urban Health's analysis of NHS data found respiratory-infection admission rates around 41% higher for under-18s in England's most deprived areas (2024/25) — and lower-income areas tend to have more pollution. Their data doesn't prove pollution is the cause; say "linked to", not "caused by".

Avoid the "400 under-5s a day" figure circulating online — it doesn't match its own source.

slides.name: When the air is bad, learning stops

layers.name: When the air is bad, learnin

params.text: When the air is bad, learning stops

layers.name: After a spike in fine partic

params.text: After a spike in fine particles (PM2.5), over the next three days:

layers.name: more pupils off school for t

params.text: more pupils off school for the whole day

layers.name: more pupils sent out of clas

params.text: more pupils sent out of class to the office
Hardest hit: low-income and younger pupils. Schools downwind of a main road see lower test scores and more absences.
Sources: Chung, Persico & Liu, NBER Working Paper 33549 (2025), a 10 µg/m³ daily rise in PM2.5, US school district; Heissel, Persico & Simon, Journal of Human Resources (2022)
THE AIR POLLUTION PROJECT  ·  MARK MARTIN MBE

slides.notes:
Pollution doesn't stay in the lungs — it reaches the timetable. Two ways learning is lost: the pupil who's at home ill, and the pupil who's in the room but can't settle.

A 2025 NBER study of a large US school district (Chung, Persico & Liu) used wind direction to isolate pollution's effect: a 10 µg/m³ rise in daily PM2.5 led to 5.7% more full-day absences and 28% more office referrals over three days, and 13% more teacher sick absences. The effects were driven by low-income and younger students. (Click for each number.)

Heissel, Persico & Simon (Journal of Human Resources, 2022): when pupils move to a school downwind of a highway, their test scores fall and behavioural incidents and absences rise, compared with an upwind school in the same area.

Be clear these are US studies; the mechanism is the same on a London school street.

slides.name: The air isn’t shared fairly

layers.name: The people who drive least b

params.text: The people who drive least breathe the most
Who drives least: no car or van at home
more NO₂ where ethnic-minority Londoners are most likely to live, than where White Londoners are

layers.name: more NO₂ in the most deprive

params.text: more NO₂ in the most deprived areas (2019)

layers.name: And every London school is i

params.text: And every London school is in an area above the WHO guideline for fine particles (PM2.5).
Sources: Department for Transport, National Travel Survey 2015–19 (via Ethnicity facts and figures); Mayor of London, Air Pollution and Inequalities in London: 2019 update (published Oct 2021)
THE AIR POLLUTION PROJECT  ·  MARK MARTIN MBE

slides.notes:
Air pollution isn't shared fairly. Campaigners call it environmental injustice: the communities that contribute least to traffic pollution breathe the most of it.

Who drives least: in England (National Travel Survey, 2015–19), 40% of Black people lived in a household with no car or van — the highest of any group — against 17% of White people.

Who breathes most: City Hall's 2019 analysis found NO₂ concentrations 16–27% higher in the areas where ethnic-minority Londoners are most likely to live than where White Londoners are, and 13% higher in the most deprived areas. The good news: those gaps have narrowed since 2013 as London's air has improved.

Click: every London school is in an area above the WHO guideline for PM2.5.

The reasons are structural — housing near main roads, less green space — which is exactly why communities need their own data.

"It can't be done." "Yes, but…" "We're not ready for that yet." "You could lose your job for that."

slides.name: So we built it

params.text: A low-cost sensor, wired up by students, logging a real London street.
THE AIR POLLUTION PROJECT  ·  MARK MARTIN MBE

slides.notes:
The turn. Say it plainly: "So we built it."

A cardboard-mounted sensor — Arduino, gas and particulate sensors — sitting on a real roadside, collecting real data. Built by students.

slides.name: The kit

params.text: Gas and particulate-matter sensors on an Arduino, with LED strips and a screen showing pollution live.
A Raspberry Pi gathers every reading, ready to be queried.
Students build their own data views and apps, and share what they find.
THE AIR POLLUTION PROJECT  ·  MARK MARTIN MBE

slides.notes:
The kit is deliberately simple and cheap.

1 · Sense: a gas sensor and a particulate-matter sensor on an Arduino (calibrated first), two LED strips that show each type of pollution, and an LCD with the readings.
2 · Collect: a Raspberry Pi talks to the Arduino over USB serial and stores the data.
3 · Tell the story: students query it and build their own views and apps.

slides.name: Ownership

layers.name: They own the problem, the da

params.text: They own the problem, the data and the answer

Build and calibrate their own sensors
Collect real data from their own streets
Analyse it with Python and pandas

THE AIR POLLUTION PROJECT  ·  MARK MARTIN MBE

slides.notes:
Ownership is the difference. Students build and calibrate the sensors, collect data from streets they walk every day, analyse it in Python and pandas, and publish it.

The aim from day one: expose students to modern data science, AI and data visualisation — and give them something real for their CV, UCAS applications, tech portfolios and careers.

slides.name: Breathe London · the backpack study

params.text: Backpacks that measure the school run
more nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) on the walk to school than in the classroom, on average
pupils in five boroughs wore Dyson sensor backpacks for a week
of families changed how they travel to school
Sources: King’s College London and Mayor of London, Breathe London Wearables Study (2019). Route drawing is illustrative.
THE AIR POLLUTION PROJECT  ·  MARK MARTIN MBE

slides.notes:
Another example of children as scientists — and it links to our partner, the James Dyson Foundation. In the Breathe London Wearables Study (2019), funded by the Mayor of London and analysed by King's College London, around 250 primary pupils from schools in Richmond, Greenwich, Haringey, Hammersmith & Fulham, and Kensington & Chelsea wore backpacks with Dyson-designed sensors for a week.

Findings: on average, children were exposed to five times more NO₂ on the school run than at school (PM2.5 was higher on the journey too). Walking along back streets gave the lowest exposure; main roads the highest. 31% of the families surveyed changed how they travel to school.

The point: once children could see their own data, families changed what they did.

slides.name: Meanwhile in Newcastle

layers.name: Residents in charge of the d

params.text: Residents in charge of the data
Worried about traffic near home or school? Communities pick the streets.
Hand-held monitors on the school run, alongside fixed ones.

layers.name: Any street can be compared w

params.text: Any street can be compared with the city, live.
Sense Explorers takes pupils’ ideas into city planning.
schools with sensors at the gate
Sources: Newcastle University press releases (2017, 2019). Photos: Newcastle University. Map: Urban Observatory, © OpenStreetMap contributors, OpenMapTiles.
THE AIR POLLUTION PROJECT  ·  MARK MARTIN MBE

slides.notes:
Ownership isn't only happening in London. In Newcastle, Sense My Street — from Newcastle University's Open Lab (2017) — put communities "in charge" of their own air data. Groups like SPACE for Heaton chose the streets and schools to test, and families collected readings with hand-held sensors on the walk to school, alongside fixed monitors.

The data feeds the Urban Observatory, which is openly available, so residents can compare their street with the city.

In 2019 Newcastle University and the City Council put NO₂ and particulate sensors outside 22 schools near major roads. Its Sense Explorers project uses the data to give children a voice in future city planning. The Observatory now runs over 3,600 sensors across Newcastle and Gateshead, adding around 5,000 observations a minute (2019 figures).

The point for our story: when residents and children own the data, they can argue for change with evidence.

Street Futures: redesign the school street

layers.name: less NO₂ on the pavement at

params.text: less NO₂ on the pavement at ARK Franklin Primary, in one student-style design

layers.name: Pick a real school. Change t

params.text: Pick a real school. Change the street. See the air.
Scenario estimate on live monitoring data, not a measured reading
THE AIR POLLUTION PROJECT  ·  MARK MARTIN MBE

slides.notes:
Back to the school street. Remember the Tower Hamlets children fighting to keep theirs? Street Futures lets any student test that argument with evidence.

Pick a real London monitoring site — several are primary schools, like ARK Franklin Primary Academy — then redesign the street: plant trees, add a kerbside hedge, a traffic filter, electrify the fleet, or make it a School Street. The model shows what happens to NO₂, PM2.5 and PM10 where a person actually stands.

Example: School Street + street trees + kerbside hedge at ARK Franklin took pavement NO₂ from 12.6 to 8.7 µg/m³ (about −31%). It's a scenario estimate on live data, so the number changes day to day. Demo it live: street-futures.vercel.app
